title: Foggy or Cloudy Between the Panes: Why a Double-Pane Window Fogs Up and How to Fix It
question: My double-pane window is permanently cloudy and foggy between the two pieces of glass, and I can't wipe it off from either side. What caused this and do I have to replace the whole window?
summary: The haze is trapped moisture inside a sealed insulated glass unit (IGU): the two panes and the airspace between them are a factory-sealed sandwich with a moisture-absorbing desiccant in the spacer, and once the perimeter seal fails and the desiccant saturates, humid air leaks in and condenses where you can't reach it. The thing most people get wrong: you almost never have to replace the whole window. In most cases only the sealed glass unit needs to be swapped, and the existing frame and sash stay. Wiping, drilling, or "defog" services are cosmetic at best; they do not restore the insulating gas or the R-value the failed seal lost.

commonCauses.cause: Normal seal aging: the perimeter seal simply wore out (most double-pane seals last about 10-20 years)
commonCauses.quickCheck: Find the metal spacer bar between the panes; many have a date stamp, or check when the windows were installed. If they're 10+ years old, age is the likely culprit.

commonCauses.cause: Heat and sun cycling ('thermal pumping'): daily expansion and contraction of the trapped air fatigues the seal, worst on south/west-facing sunny windows
commonCauses.quickCheck: Note whether the fogged windows face the sun and get hot. If your failed units cluster on the sunny side of the house, cycling stress is the driver.

commonCauses.cause: Standing water or blocked weep holes at the sill keeping the seal wet, which rots it from the outside in
commonCauses.quickCheck: Look at the bottom outside edge of the glass and the sill. Check for pooled water, failed caulk, or clogged weep holes; a chronically wet lower seal fails first.

commonCauses.cause: Manufacturing defect or a bad/undersized desiccant fill causing early failure while still fairly new
commonCauses.quickCheck: If the window is only a few years old and fogged, it's likely a defect; pull the maker/date stamp and check the warranty (many IGUs carry a 10-20 year sealed-unit warranty).

commonCauses.cause: Physical stress: house settling, a racked frame, or rough handling that flexed the glass and broke the seal
commonCauses.quickCheck: Look for a frame that's out of square, sticking sashes, or a chipped/pinched glass edge near the fog, which points to mechanical stress rather than age.

fixes: Confirm the fog is actually between the panes: wipe both the inside and the outside glass surfaces with a clean dry cloth. If the haze stays put and can't be reached, the seal has failed internally; that's an IGU problem, not a cleaning problem.

Check the warranty first. Find the maker and date stamp (etched in a glass corner or printed on the metal spacer), locate your install paperwork, and call the manufacturer; sealed units often carry a 10-20 year warranty and a replacement IGU may be free or heavily discounted.

Understand your three real options before spending money: (a) replace only the sealed glass unit and keep the frame/sash, usually the best value; (b) replace the entire window (only if the frame is rotted or you want an energy upgrade); (c) a cosmetic 'defog' service that drills and clears the haze but does NOT restore the seal, gas fill, or insulation value, so treat it as a stopgap, not a repair.

Measure the glass precisely for a replacement IGU: width, height, and the overall unit thickness (edge to edge through both panes, commonly around 1/2 to 1 inch). Note whether it has a Low-E coating (a faint tint/reflection). Critically, check for a safety-glass etch, a small 'tempered' mark or manufacturer 'bug' stamped in a glass corner: if the original is tempered you MUST order tempered again. Code (IRC R308) requires safety glazing in and next to doors, in windows close to the floor, and near tubs/showers/stairs; when unsure, match the original and confirm with the glass shop.

Order the replacement IGU from a local glass shop or window dealer, matching the exact size, thickness, Low-E coating, and gas fill (typically argon), and specifying tempered glass wherever safety glazing is required or the original was tempered. Expect a lead time of roughly 1-3 weeks for a custom unit.
For an operable, removable sash on a ground-floor window (DIY-friendly): take the whole sash out and lay it flat on a padded surface so you're never wrestling glass at height.

Remove the glazing stops or beads that hold the glass in. Score the paint/sealant line with a utility knife first, then gently pry the stops out with a putty knife or trim tool, keeping them intact to reuse. In pre-1980s windows the old glazing putty, sealant, and paint can contain asbestos or lead: do not dry-scrape or sand them; keep the material damp and intact, follow lead-safe/asbestos-safe handling, or have it tested (or the job done by a certified pro) before disturbing it. Lift out the old IGU using two suction cup grips.

Clean the glazing channel, set the new IGU on fresh setting blocks (never glass directly on the frame), bed it with glazing tape or a compatible sealant, and reinstall the stops. Re-caulk the exterior perimeter with a quality exterior silicone and clear any clogged weep holes so water drains.
For fixed picture windows, large/heavy panes, upper-floor windows, or units glazed from the outside, stop and hire a glazier; see the DIY-vs-pro guidance.

If the frame itself is rotted, the window is old and single-glazed anyway, or you want lower energy bills, price a full window replacement instead of just the glass and weigh it against the IGU-only cost.

If you choose the cosmetic defog route, set expectations: it clears the visible haze but leaves the airspace vented, so insulation value is reduced and fog can return; it's a temporary, appearance-only fix.

Verify the repair: after install, the new unit should be perfectly clear with no haze, stay clear through a warm day and a cold night (a temperature swing that would re-fog a bad seal), and have intact, watertight exterior caulk.
diyVsPro: DIY is reasonable for a ground-floor, operable window whose sash you can lift out and lay flat, with removable glazing stops and a small-to-medium glass unit you can safely handle; measuring, ordering the IGU, and swapping it is within reach for a careful homeowner. Stop and call a licensed glazier or window installer if any of these apply: the window is on an upper floor or requires working at height (fall risk), the pane is large or heavy enough to need more than two people, the glass is a fixed/picture unit or is glazed from the outside, safety (tempered) glass is required and you're unsure how to source or handle it, the frame or surrounding wall shows rot or water damage, the home predates the mid-1980s and you'd be disturbing old glazing putty or paint (possible asbestos/lead), or the glass is already cracked. Full-frame window replacement is a pro job. When in doubt about size, weight, or height, hire it out: broken tempered glass and falls cause serious injury.
typicalCostUSD: Glass-only (IGU) replacement: roughly $150-$600 per window installed by a pro, or about $50-$250 for a DIY-sourced small-to-medium unit; large, Low-E, or tempered units run higher. Full window replacement: about $300-$1,200+ per window installed. Cosmetic defog service: roughly $75-$200 per window (appearance only, seal not restored). A valid manufacturer warranty can drop the glass cost to near zero.
timeEstimate: Measuring and ordering: about 30-60 minutes, then 1-3 weeks lead time for a custom IGU. The actual glass swap on a removable sash: roughly 30-90 minutes per window for a DIYer.
safetyNote: The main hazards are glass and height, not electrical or gas. Wear cut-resistant gloves and eye protection any time you handle or remove glass: edges cut deeply and a sealed unit can shatter. Large panes are heavy and awkward; use suction-cup grips and a two-person lift, and lay the sash flat rather than working vertically. Do NOT work on upper-floor or hard-to-reach windows from a ladder; fall risk makes that a pro job. In homes built before 1978, painted window frames and sashes may contain lead paint, and window glazing putty and caulk made before the mid-1980s may contain asbestos; do not dry-sand or scrape either, keep the material damp and intact, and follow EPA lead-safe (RRP) practices and asbestos-safe handling, or hire a certified pro, if that material will be disturbed. If you find frame rot with soft, discolored wood or persistent moisture, check for hidden water intrusion and mold behind the trim before sealing anything back up; areas of mold larger than about 10 square feet should be handled by a professional. Dispose of the old glass unit wrapped and labeled so no one is cut.
toolsParts: Made-to-measure replacement insulated glass unit (IGU), matching size, thickness, Low-E coating, gas fill, and tempered rating where required
Putty knife and a stiff trim/glazing removal tool
Glazing tape or compatible glazing sealant
Exterior-grade silicone caulk and a caulk gun
Replacement glazing stops or beads (if the originals break)
Shop vacuum for cleaning the glazing channel
Padded work surface or moving blanket to lay the sash flat
